Stage 2 · Bengaluru terrain map · Real public data: satellite elevation and OpenStreetMap

Bengaluru's ground: valley and ridge.

The real city, classified with the same rule as the simulated one: a spot is valley ground if it sits lower than the average within 1.5 km, ridge ground if higher. There are no wells on this map yet: the real wells' locations are not available. Click anywhere to see the terrain values a well at that spot would give the model.

City area classified—inside the city boundary, lakes excluded
Valley ground—the rest is ridge; a relative measure, so near half by design
Lakes of 1 hectare or more—
Ground height—above sea level, 1st to 99th percentile
Valley ground Ridge ground Lake Stronger colour: more clearly low or high

Click anywhere in the city

The panel shows the ground at that spot: valley or ridge, height, how far it sits above or below its surroundings, slope, and the distance to the nearest lake. These are the terrain values the model would use as a starting guess for a well there.

Elevation: Copernicus DEM (GLO-30), © DLR e.V. 2010–2014 and © Airbus Defence and Space GmbH 2014–2018, provided under COPERNICUS by the European Union and ESA. Street map, city boundaries and lakes: © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the ODbL. Map viewer: Leaflet.

By city corporation

Bengaluru has been run by five city corporations since 2025. Each has a similar mix of valley and ridge ground, because the measure compares every spot with its own surroundings.

What this map is not
  • Not a prediction for any real well. "Valley wells recover fast, ridge wells slowly" is how our simulator was built, not something yet checked for Bengaluru.
  • Fractured rock is missing. No open fracture-line map was available; the Geological Survey's maps can be viewed online but not downloaded as data.
  • Roofs are in the elevation. The satellite model measures the top surface, buildings and trees included. It was smoothed over about 150 m, which removes single buildings but not whole dense districts.
  • No wells. The 579 real wells have no locations yet.
What would make it a real tool
  • Well locations, or the data holder running our script to return each well's terrain values. The model then gets a real starting guess for every well.
  • A fracture-line map from the Geological Survey of India, or a pumping test on a few wells.
  • Bare-earth elevation (for example FABDEM, which removes buildings and trees) and a paved-share map (ESA WorldCover), both public.
  • Checking the valley/ridge link against the first real water levels. See the simulated city it came from →
Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: vendor export (15 days, July 2026, in the vendor's real format but with demonstration water-level values), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (physics-based simulations of the 579 wells: one year in iteration 1, five years in later iterations and in Stage 2). No real water-level measurement has been used yet, and nothing here is yet a validated field forecast. Built by the FARII consortium.
